title.en: The Origin of Death: Raven Outvotes Coyote
title.zh: 死亡之起源：渡鴉否決郊狼

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (1) The Origin of Death' (Thompson, collected by Teit)

summary.en: Coyote the traveller finds Raven, a selfish chief who wants long winters, all the game, and mortal men. Coyote pleads that death brings sorrow and proposes death like sleep with return; Raven and his followers — Crow, Fly, Maggot — demand final death so they may feed on corpses. Coyote concedes that people shall die when their time comes, but only until the world changes again. Soon Raven's own daughter sickens and dies, the first death, and her desperate father begs to undo the decree; Coyote answers that it is settled and cannot be altered.
summary.zh: 郊狼行旅，遇自私酋長渡鴉；彼欲嚴冬、獨佔獵物，且不欲人長生。郊狼陳說死亡之苦，倡『死如眠、可復返』；渡鴉與其黨羽——鴉、蠅、蛆——卻要人永死，以便食屍。郊狼終允：人屆期而亡，然至世界再變之時將不再死。未幾渡鴉之女病死，是為首亡；渡鴉哀求更改，郊狼答：事已定，不可易。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson (Nlaka'pamux) narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only; no restricted ceremonial knowledge. Category 'myth'. Messenger-debate variant of the origin-of-death cluster.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to Raven, a bad, selfish chief, who wanted to make everything difficult for other people and easy for himself. He wanted the game for himself, wanted long winters, and did not want man to be immortal. Coyote questioned him why he wanted people to die; Raven said, 'If people were immortal, there would be too many. Let them become sick and die.' Coyote said death would introduce sorrow into the world: 'Let them be sick, but not die.' But Raven's people supported their chief, and Crow, Fly, Maggot and many others clamored for people to die, so that they might feed on corpses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 1 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote proposed, 'Let people die for a while, and then come to life again. Let death be like sleep.' Raven answered, 'No; if they die, let them die for good, and let their bodies rot.' At last Coyote agreed: 'Well, it is ordained that people shall die when their time has come. Their bodies shall be buried, and their souls shall go to the spirit-land; but this will only be until the world changes again, when they will die no more.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 1 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Shortly after that, Raven's daughter became sick and died — she was the first to die. Raven tried to restore her to life, but failed, and wept. He went to Coyote and said, 'Let us change what we said before. Do not let people die and remain dead forever!' Coyote answered, 'No, it is settled now, and cannot be altered.' Thus it happens that people die and are buried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 1 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Steals Fire: The Dancing Head-Dress and the Burning Country

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (2) Coyote Steals Fire' (Thompson, collected by Teit)

summary.en: From a mountain top Coyote sees a light far to the south, learns from his own excrements that it is fire, and sets out with Fox, Wolf, Antelope and all the good runners. They dance with the Fire people, Coyote in a head-dress of pitchy pine shavings with long cedar-bark fringes; when the fire blazes high, his fringes catch, he runs out swinging them through the flames, and the fire is carried in relays by the runners while the Fire people kill them one by one. Coyote gives the fire to a tree, hides as dung, and escapes through smoke; the spreading fire burns many people until Coyote brings rain and flood to quench it. Since then fire is in wood: cedar-bark carries fire, pitch-wood kindles, and smoke always signs fire.
summary.zh: 郊狼自山頂見南方遠光，問於己糞，知其為火，遂與狐、狼、羚羊等善跑者同行盜火。眾與火族共舞，郊狼戴松脂刨花冠、垂雪松皮長纓；火旺時冠纓著火，他揮纓掠火而逃，眾接力傳火，火族逐一誅之。郊狼以火授樹，化糞藏身，冒煙得脫；火燎原，焚斃多人，郊狼召雨洪滅火。自此火藏於木：雪松皮可攜火，松脂易燃，煙常為火之兆。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'. Fire-theft cluster parallel.

passages.text: From the top of a mountain Coyote saw a light far away to the south. He did not know what it was; he defecated and questioned his excrements, and they said, 'That is fire.' He made up his mind to go and get it, and many people accompanied him — Fox, Wolf, Antelope, and all the good runners. When they reached the house of the Fire people, they told them, 'We have come to visit you, to dance, to play, and to gamble.' The Fire people danced first, with the fire very low; then Coyote's people danced in a circle around it, complaining that they could not see, until the fire blazed up high.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 2 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote's people pretended to be very hot and went out to cool themselves, taking up positions for running; only Coyote remained, dancing about wildly until his head-dress of pitchy yellow-pine shavings with its long fringes of dry cedar-bark took fire. He pretended to be afraid and asked the Fire people to put it out; when near the door he swung the burning fringes across the fire and ran out. The Fire people pursued; he gave the head-band to Antelope, and the fire was carried in relays, the pursuers killing the runners one by one until only Coyote was left. He ran behind a tree and gave the fire to it, then changed himself into dung; the Fire people found nothing, and wind-driven sparks set the grass ablaze.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 2 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fire spread all over the country and burned up many people. Coyote caused a heavy rainfall and a flood, which put it out. After this the fire was in the trees, and grass and trees could be used for making fire: dry cedar-bark carries fire and serves for slow-matches, pitch-wood ignites easily for starting fires, and since then smoke and fire have been inseparable in the world — smoke is always a sign of fire, and wind makes fire blaze, which is why people blow on fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 2 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Tames the Elk: Teaching the People to Hunt

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (3) Coyote and Elk' (Thompson, collected by Teit)

summary.en: After introducing the salmon, Coyote comes to a country whose people cannot hunt: they kill only with clubs and stones, the game fears them not at all, and some animals hunt and eat people. Refugees flee from Elk, who hunts men as they hunt deer. Coyote meets Bull Elk 'hunting for my wives,' asks if he kills people, and transforms him into a common elk — 'Henceforth people shall hunt and kill you.' Then he teaches the people to make bows and arrows, to hunt, cut up and cure meat, and to dress skins.
summary.zh: 郊狼既授鮭，行至獵術未開之國：其民唯以棍石擊獸，獸不畏人，甚者反獵食人。民逃避麋鹿。郊狼遇公麋自稱『獵吾妻』，問其食人否，答『間或為之』，遂化之為凡獸：『自此人獵汝而殺汝。』復教民製弓矢、獵獸、剖肉、治皮、乾藏。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: After Coyote had introduced the salmon, made fishing-utensils, and shown the people how to fish, prepare, and cure salmon, he went to another country. The people there did not know how to hunt: they used clubs and stones, and obtained very little game, for the animals were not afraid of them — often the game chased the people, and some kinds of game even hunted and ate people. One day Coyote met some people running, and they said, 'Elk is hunting us. He will kill and eat us.' Coyote asked why they did not kill him, and they answered, 'We are afraid. He is more powerful than we are.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 3 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote went on and soon met a Bull Elk, and asked him where he was going. 'I am hunting for my wives,' said the elk. 'Do you kill people?' asked Coyote, and he answered, 'Yes, sometimes.' Coyote transformed him into a common elk, saying, 'Henceforth people shall hunt and kill you.' Then he taught the people how to make bows and arrows, how to hunt, cut up, and cure meat, and how to dress skins; after this they hunted deer and other game.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 3 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote, Fox, and the Sun People's Bag
title.zh: 郊狼、狐狸與太陽族的袋子

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (5) Coyote, Fox, and the Sun People' (Thompson, collected by Teit)

summary.en: Travelling near the Sun's house, Coyote and Fox find a bag hanging from a pole and cannot tell what is inside. Fox's pipe answers 'Sun-rays,' Coyote's excrements answer 'hot wind.' Fox shoots a large-pointed arrow and bursts the bag: sun-rays and hot wind pour out with a great noise, and the two flee with the Sun people chasing them — until they turn, threaten to shoot, and the frightened Sun people run home.
summary.zh: 郊狼與狐近太陽之屋而行，見竿頭懸囊，不知何物。狐抽煙問卜，答『日光』；郊狼問糞，答『熱風』。狐以大鏃箭射爆其囊，日光熱風轟然而出，二人奔逃，太陽族人追之；二人回首威嚇欲射，追逐者懼而返家。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox were travelling and went near the Sun's house. There they saw a bag hanging from the end of a pole, and neither could tell what was in it. Fox smoked his pipe and questioned it, and the pipe answered, 'Sun-rays.' Coyote defecated and questioned his excrements, and they answered, 'Hot wind.' The two disputed as to who was right. Fox told Coyote to pull down the bag; Coyote tried in vain to reach it, tried to push over the pole, and finally pierced it at the bottom with his arrow-flaker, making a small hole through which something bright came out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 4 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Fox said, 'That must be a sun-ray; pull it down!' Coyote took hold of it and burned his hand, so Fox hit the bag with a large-pointed arrow and burst it. Then the hot wind and the sun-rays came out with a great noise, and Coyote and Fox ran away, pursued by the people of the lodge. When they were nearly overtaken, they turned around and threatened to shoot the Sun people, who at once became afraid and ran back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 4 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Teaches People to Mate

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (6) Coyote teaches People to mate' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Coyote comes to a country where men and women know not how to propagate, and shows them how to mate; the women will not let him go until he is thoroughly fatigued, and when he runs away they chase him. After that the women of that country bear children.
summary.zh: 郊狼行至男女不識生育之國，示以婚配之道；眾女不放其行，直待他力竭方止；他遁走，眾女追之。此後該國婦女始能誕育子女。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Brief culture-hero episode on the origin of procreation, paraphrased plainly. Published folk-narrative only; no ceremonial content. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to a country where lived men and women who knew not how to propagate. He showed them how to mate. The women would not let him go until he was thoroughly fatigued; then he ran away, and they chased him. After that the women of that country bore children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 4 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Marmots of the Clashing Rocks

region.en: Mountain pass, Upper Salmon River, Thompson country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上薩爾蒙河山隘，湯普森人故地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (7) Coyote and the Marmots' (Thompson)

summary.en: Two marmots guard a mountain pass from behind rocks, clashing them together on every traveller until nothing can pass through but the wind. Coyote enters the pass; as the rocks begin to close he wedges his antler arrow-flaker across, holds the gap, transforms the marmots into animals and the moving rocks into stationary cliffs — the narrow passage between two cliffs through which the trail runs to this day.
summary.zh: 兩隻旱獺匿石後守山隘，凡有行者，即合石擊斃，唯風可過。郊狼入隘；當石欲合時，以鹿角整箭器橫撐其間，石不得合；遂化旱獺為獸、化活動之石為屹立巖崖——今小道所經兩崖間之窄徑即其遺。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote came to a pass in the mountains — some say on Upper Salmon River — inhabited by two Marmots, who sat one on each side behind rocks. When people passed through, they clashed the rocks together and killed them; nothing could pass through except the wind. Coyote heard of them and determined to pass through. When he was in the middle, the rocks began to shut; but he placed his antler arrow-flaker across, and they could not shut. He transformed the Marmots into animals, and the rocks into stationary cliffs. There is a narrow passage between two cliffs, through which the trail passes now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 4 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Attacked by Comb and Awl: The Tools Enslaved
title.zh: 梳與錐襲郊狼：器物淪為奴

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (8) Coyote is attacked by Comb and Awl' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Entering a tidy underground lodge where no one is visible, Coyote covets its fine things: the comb combs him violently, the awl pierces him, the smoothing-stones jump and scratch off his skin, and the stone hammer stuns him with a blow to the head. Beaten, he runs away crying the decree that turns them into mere tools: 'Henceforth you shall be mere tools and slaves of people.'
summary.zh: 郊狼入一整潔之地下屋，屋中無人而物什井然。他貪取美梳，梳即狂梳其身；取錐，錐即刺之；取磨箭石，石跳動抓剝其皮；取石錘，錘重擊其首，昏厥而逃。逃時怒下咒令：『自此爾等不得為人、不得傷人，只為凡器、為人之奴。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote came to an underground lodge, which he entered. He saw no one inside; but everything looked in order, as if people lived there — bows and arrows, quivers, war-clubs, baskets, and bags. He picked up a nice comb and examined it, and thought he would take it. As he turned to go away he heard people murmuring; looking around, he saw nothing. As he started to climb the ladder, the comb scratched and combed him violently. 'Stop! I will put you back,' he said. Then he thought he would take an awl: again the murmuring, and as he started to run away, the awl pierced him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 4-5 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He took a pair of fine stones for smoothing arrows, and they attacked him, jumping up and down and scratching off his skin. Lastly he took a stone hammer, and it hit him so hard on the head that he was stunned, and ran away. Angry, he cried out: 'You shall no longer be people and have power to attack: henceforth you shall be mere tools and slaves of people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 5 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Geese: Carried Up by the Flock
title.zh: 郊狼與雁：被雁群捲上半空

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (9) Coyote and the Geese' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Coyote cuts a club and whistles a flock of geese out of the sky, claps his hands, and they all fall down; but when he clubs them among the cackling, flapping birds, the wings raise such a wind that he is lifted off his feet and carried away, missing first the swamp-grass, then the willows, then the tree-tops, until he drops head-first into the middle of a swamp. Mosquitoes and flies bite him and crawl into him, and at last Fox comes along and pulls him out.
summary.zh: 郊狼削棍吹哨，群雁盤旋而降；拍掌一響，盡落於地。他執棍亂擊，雁聲撲翼釀成大風，竟將他掀上半空，先抓沼草不得、再抓柳梢不得、復抓樹梢不得，終倒栽於沼心泥中不得自拔。蚊蠅噬之，鑽入其身。後狐狸至，方拔之出。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling through a country of lakes and swamps. He saw a large flock of geese flying overhead and wished he could kill and eat them. He cut a club of wood, and whistled; they halted, and circled around. He clapped his hands, and they all fell down. He ran among them and clubbed them; but they merely cackled, laughed, and flapped their wings, and in the noise and confusion he could not see where he was hitting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 5 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wings caused a strong wind, and as they rose Coyote was taken off his feet and carried along by them. He caught at the swamp-grass tops, then at the willow-bush tops, then at the tree tops, but could not hold on. He was carried to a point above the middle of a near-by swamp, where he dropped head first into the mud and could not extricate himself. The mosquitoes, flies, and insects bit his legs and his backside and crawled into him. At last Fox came along and pulled him out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 5 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote, Fox, and the Egg-Gatherers

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (10) Coyote, Fox, and the Egg-Gatherers' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: While Coyote and Fox sleep off a fat meal, mischievous women tickle them with feathers and exchange their noses. When they wake each laughs at the other's face — and it is only at the lake, seeing their reflections, that they realize their own faces were changed too; they quarrel, each blaming the other, until they hear people laughing and know a trick was played. Following the tracks, they find the women gathering ducks' eggs in a swamp.
summary.zh: 郊狼與狐食肥酣睡，戲弄之婦以羽搔癢，並互換二獸之鼻。二人醒後互笑對方之臉，及至湖邊照影，方知己顏亦遭改換；遂互相指責爭吵，直至聞人笑聲，始知被戲。循足跡而去，見婦人正於沼中拾鴨蛋。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox had cooked some fat meat, and, after eating, fell sound asleep. Some women who found them asleep thought they would have some fun with them. They tickled them with feathers, but the two slept on; then they changed their noses. When the two awoke, they laughed at each other, but neither thought his own face had also been changed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 5-6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thirsty because they had eaten so much fat, they went down to a lake to drink; and when they saw by their reflections how ugly they had become, they quarrelled, each blaming the other for being the cause of his changed appearance. They heard people laughing, and then knew that a trick had been played on them. They followed the tracks of the women, and saw them busy gathering ducks' eggs in a swamp.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and his Guest: The Broken Beak

region.en: Spences Bridge, Thompson River, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斯賓塞斯布里奇，湯普森河，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (11) Coyote and his Guests' (Thompson, from Spences Bridge)

summary.en: Coyote feasts at Kingfisher's lodge, where his host dives through a hole in the ice with a withe and brings up fish four times. On returning the visit, Coyote fits a pitch-wood beak to his nose, climbs a tree over a shallow waterhole, gives the kingfisher's cry — and breaks his nose and his head in the hole. Kingfisher laughs at the bungling guest, then catches fish for him so they may eat.
summary.zh: 郊狼赴翠鳥之宴，見主人持藤條自冰洞潛水，四度銜魚而歸，飽食而去。回請之日，郊狼黏松脂木為喙於鼻，攀樹臨淺水窟，學翠鳥啼而俯衝——鼻首俱碎。翠鳥笑其拙，仍捕魚相饗。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Bungling-host episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once upon a time Coyote visited Kingfisher. Since Kingfisher had no food, he went out carrying a withe, climbed a tree, uttered the Kingfisher's cry, and dived through a hole in the ice; soon he emerged carrying a fish, and repeated this four times. He strung the fish on the withe, returned to the lodge, and cooked them for Coyote, who ate until he was satiated. On leaving, Coyote invited Kingfisher to visit him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Kingfisher entered Coyote's house, he saw nothing to eat. Coyote went out, cut a willow withe to carry the fish, fitted to his nose a long piece of pitch-wood to serve as a beak, and climbed a tree overhanging a shallow hole from which he used to draw water. He uttered the Kingfisher's cry and dived down into the hole, where he broke his nose and his head. Kingfisher laughed at the bungling Coyote, then caught some fish for him so that they might eat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and his Elk Wife

region.en: Nicola country, Thompson land, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉之地，湯普森人鄉土，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (12) Coyote and his Elk Wife' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Elk chief gives Coyote one of his daughters to wife, with a rule: she may be bitten on the rump for meat, the wound healing each time, but not before four nights, and never more than once a day. Coyote, hungry on the road north, breaks the rule; his wife runs away and becomes an elk living in the Nicola country, and ever since elks have been numerous there.
summary.zh: 麋酋以女妻郊狼，且立規：餓時可齧其妻臀部為食，創口自癒；惟四夜之前不得咬，此後每日不得逾一次。郊狼北行飢甚，破戒而咬；妻奔逃，化為麋居尼古拉之地。自此該地麋群繁盛。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote had been travelling somewhere to the south, where he met Elk chief, who gave him one of his daughters to wife, telling him: 'If you are hungry, you may take a bite of meat from your wife's rump, which will heal over each time. However, you must not bite her before four nights have passed, and after that not more than once a day.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Travelling north, Coyote had reached the Nicola country; he hunted on the way, but could get no game, and was hungry. 'Why should I have an Elk wife and not eat her?' he said. 'Why should I wait when I am hungry?' He snapped at his wife, but she ran away; he followed and coaxed her back. In the evening, when they camped, he jumped at his wife and bit her. She ran away and became an elk that lived in the Nicola country. Coyote went on alone and came to the Thompson River; ever since that time elks have been numerous in the Nicola country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Digs Roots in the Sky Country

region.en: Sky country above the Thompson lands (symbolic pin at Nicola Valley)
region.zh: 湯普森人故地上空之天國（象徵定位於尼古拉谷）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (14) Coyote digs Roots' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Hungry and seeing no lodges or people, Coyote cuts a root-digger and digs a large tatu'En root; wind rushes up through the hole, and he can see people walking far below. He puts the plant back and digs another with the same result — for he must have been in the sky country, and those roots were stars.
summary.zh: 郊狼飢而四顧無人煙，削枝為掘根杖，掘得大株 tatu'En 根；風自穴中上衝，他俯視竟見極下方行人往來。復土掩之，再掘一株，其象依然——蓋其所處乃天國，而其所掘之『根』實為星辰。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Sky-world episode; the pin is symbolic. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to a country where many tatu'En roots grew. He was hungry, and could find no game, nor could he see any lodges or people. He cut a stick to serve as a root-digger, and said, 'I will dig some roots and eat them.' He saw a large one and dug it out; wind rushed up through the hole, and he could see people walking way down below. He put the plant back again. He dug another one, and the same thing happened. He must have been in the sky country, and these roots were stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 7 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Fox Steals Coyote's Food: The Rock that Held Him
title.zh: 狐竊郊狼之食：困人之石

region.en: Lower Nicola Valley, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 下尼古拉谷，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (15) Fox steals Coyote's Food' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Waiting for his ground-squirrels to bake, Coyote sits on a rock, leans back and falls asleep; the rock holds him fast while Fox eats every squirrel. Released at last, Coyote finds Fox asleep in tall grass and fires the grass — but Fox escapes through the smoke, his skin scorched: since then the fox is reddish. The hollowed stone with Coyote's seat-marks still lies in the Lower Nicola Valley.
summary.zh: 郊狼烤松鼠以待熟，坐石倚之而眠；石困其身，狐竟食盡松鼠。久之方脫，尋狐於高草間縱火焚之；狐自煙中遁，皮已烙赤——狐之赤色由此。下尼古拉谷今猶存中空之石，上有郊狼坐痕與立痕。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote killed some young ground-squirrels and made a hole in which to bake them. He stood waiting for them to be done; then, feeling tired, he sat down on a rock near by, leaned back, and fell asleep. When he woke up, he saw Fox eating the squirrels. He tried to get up, but the rock held him. 'Leave some for me, Brother Fox!' — but Fox ate all the squirrels and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 7 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a long time Coyote was released, and gave chase to Fox, finding him asleep in some tall grass. He set fire to the grass and thought he had killed him, but Fox escaped in the smoke, his skin scorched; since then the fox has been of a reddish color. The stone on which Coyote lay may still be seen in the Lower Nicola Valley, hollowed in the middle, with the mark of Coyote's seat on a stone near by and the marks of his feet on another. It is not known who released Coyote: some say Fox made the stone seize him and afterwards let him go; some say the stone never seized him, but that Fox caused him to stick to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 7-8 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Fox Steals Coyote's Food: The Tree that Fell

region.en: Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (16) Fox steals Coyote's Food' (Thompson)

summary.en: Half-brothers who play tricks on each other: Coyote cooks a carcass in a pit and naps under a branchy tree; Fox comes along and makes the tree fall on him, trapping him while the meat is eaten to the last morsel before Coyote can work free.
summary.zh: 郊狼與狐為異父兄弟（或表親），慣相捉弄。郊狼烹獸於坑，臥枝繁樹下小憩；狐至，令樹倒壓之。郊狼被困之際，狐將肉食盡，待其掙脫，片甲無存。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox were half-brothers (or cousins). They often played tricks on each other. Once Coyote had found a carcass (or had killed some game), which he began to cook in a pit; while he was waiting under a branchy tree for the meat to be done, he fell asleep. Fox came along and caused the tree to fall on Coyote, who could not get away for a time. While he was imprisoned, he saw Fox eating the meat, and begged him to leave some; but Fox ate it all before Coyote could get away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 8 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Wears Fox's Rattle

region.en: Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (17) Coyote wears Fox's Rattle' (Thompson)

summary.en: Fox fastens a rattle to his tail, warns Coyote it is dangerous and that only he can wear it — and Coyote insists. Fox ties it on with a warning not to go through brush, knowing Coyote will do exactly that; the rattle snags in the bushes and pulls out his entrails. Fox returns, takes the rattle, puts the entrails back, kicks Coyote awake — and Coyote believes he has been asleep.
summary.zh: 狐縛鈴於尾，告誡郊狼此物危險，唯彼能戴；郊狼固請。狐為其繫上，並囑勿穿叢莽——明知其必犯。郊狼穿林，鈴為枝椏所鉤，竟拽出其腸。狐至，取鈴、納腸、踢其醒；郊狼醒後猶自以為方才熟睡。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Another time Fox fastened a rattle to his tail, and Coyote wanted to get it. Fox told him it was dangerous, and that only he himself could wear it; but Coyote persisted, so Fox fastened it to Coyote's tail and warned him not to go through any brush — knowing that Coyote would try to go through brush in order to learn why this had been forbidden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 8 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote walked through bushes and stripped the rattle from his tail. He felt something pulling at his backside, and discovered that the rattle had caught in the bushes and was pulling out his entrails. He did not know what to do, and fainted. Fox came along, took away the rattle, and put back Coyote's entrails. Then he kicked Coyote, who awoke and believed that he had been asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 8 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Woodpeckers

region.en: Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (18) Coyote and the Woodpeckers' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Trapped in a cave (some say a hollow tree), Coyote calls all the animals and birds to his aid; all fail, until the woodpeckers take over — one cracks the rock, a second widens the crack, a third widens it further, and the Red-Headed Woodpecker splits it open so Coyote escapes. Some tellers add that the birds pulled him out by the tail.
summary.zh: 郊狼困於穴中（或云空心樹），呼百獸百鳥相救，皆無功；最後啄木鳥上陣：其一啄裂巖石，二鳥繼之擴裂，三鳥再擴，紅頭啄木鳥終劈石而開，郊狼得脫。或云眾鳥銜尾拽之而出。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was caught in a cave, and called on all animals and birds for aid. They tried to release him, but failed. Finally he called on the Woodpeckers: one of them struck the rock and cracked it; the second widened the crack; the third one widened it still more; and finally the Red-Headed Woodpecker split it open, so that Coyote was able to get out. Some people say Coyote was caught in a hollow tree, and that the Woodpeckers pecked a hole and took him out; some add that they pulled him out by the tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 8-9 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Giant Mosquitoes Tamed

region.en: Swamp edge, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 沼邊，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (19) The Mosquitoes' (Thompson)

summary.en: Formerly mosquitoes were large, fierce, and ate people. Mosquito and his wife lived at the edge of the timber near a swamp, hunting human prey — he took only women, his wife only men, and they preferred the blood from the privates. Coyote (or some other transformer) turned them into the small insects of today, decreeing that they should frequent swamps and woods, suck only a little blood, and never again have power to kill people.
summary.zh: 古時蚊體巨大、兇殘食人。蚊夫婦居林緣沼畔，獵人吮血——夫專獵女子，妻專獵男子，尤嗜下體之血。郊狼（或其他變形者）化之為今日之小蚊，且令：『自此爾等往來沼林，僅能吮微血，不得再殺人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Formerly mosquitoes were very large, fierce, and ate people. Mosquito and his wife lived in a house at the edge of the timber, near a swamp. They hunted people and killed them by sucking their blood; Mosquito hunted only women, and his wife hunted only men. Coyote (or some other transformer) turned them into mosquitoes, saying: 'Henceforth you shall be small insects, and shall frequent swamps and woods. You shall be able to suck a little blood only. You shall not have power to kill people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 9 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cannibal Who Used an Elk as a Decoy

region.en: Lakeshore flat, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湖岸平地，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (20) The Cannibal who used an Elk as a Decoy' (Thompson)

summary.en: A cannibal lives in a large hollow tree beside a lake, keeping a stuffed elk-skin within arrow range on the open flat; when a hunter stalks the decoy, the cannibal shoots and eats him, and many bones and skulls lie around the tree's base. Coyote defecates and makes his excrements whistle; when the cannibal looks out of the tree-top to see who is there, Coyote slips in and shoots him from behind.
summary.zh: 食人魔居湖畔大空心樹，於箭程之內曠地置填草麥皮麋為餌；獵人窺麋，即遭其射殺吞食，樹下白骨纍纍。郊狼便溺並令己糞作哨聲；魔自樹頂探首張望之際，郊狼潛入樹中，自後一箭斃之。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote (or some other transformer) was travelling, and came to a place where a cannibal lived in a large hollow tree. He used as a decoy a stuffed elk-skin, kept within arrow range on an open flat near a lake-shore. When a hunter stalked the elk, the cannibal shot and ate him; many bones and skulls were around the base of the tree. Coyote defecated, and made his excrements whistle. When the cannibal looked out of the top of the tree, thinking some one was there, Coyote entered the tree and shot the cannibal, hitting him from behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 9 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Steals the Sweat-House-Man's Blanket

region.en: Creek-side sweat house, Thompson country (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 溪畔汗屋，湯普森人故地（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (21) Coyote steals Sweat-House-Man's Blanket' (Thompson)

summary.en: Finding a fine blanket covering an apparently empty sweat house, Coyote carries it off — but something invisible follows, strikes his legs, knocks him down, blinds him and rolls him about until he loses consciousness: it is Sweat-House-Man, or the Wind, come to punish him. He wakes in the middle of a swamp, bruised, bleeding, stung by mosquitoes, sand-flies infesting mouth, nose, ears and hair, and can barely crawl out; the blanket returns to its owner.
summary.zh: 郊狼見汗屋覆以美毯，內似無人，遂攜毯而逃。行不多遠，無形者自後追擊：擊其腿、倒其身、蔽其目、翻滾其體至不省人事——乃汗屋之人（或即風神）前來懲罰。醒時已在沼心，遍體鱗傷，蚊噬蟲鑽，口鼻耳髮皆為沙蠅所據，掙扎良久方出泥沼；毯則物歸原主。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to a creek, where he saw a sweat-house covered with a nice blanket. He listened, but heard nothing except the noise sometimes made by hot stones. He lifted up a corner of the blanket, looked in, saw no one, thought, 'I will take this blanket,' and went off with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 9 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he had gone some distance, he heard a noise behind; he looked and saw nothing, but the noise came nearer until it became so terrible that Coyote started to run. Something knocked him down, picked him up again, struck his head and blinded him; he seemed to be torn to pieces and was rolled about until he lost consciousness. It was Sweat-House-Man, or the Wind, come to punish Coyote. When he woke, he found himself in the middle of a swamp, bruised and bleeding, stung by mosquitoes, his eyes and body swollen; sand-flies had crawled into his mouth, nose, ears, and hair. He extricated himself with difficulty and after tiresome travelling in the mud came out of the swamp; the blanket went back to Sweat-House-Man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 9-10 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Rolling Bowlder

region.en: Upper Uta'mqt (Lillooet) and Nicola Valley country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上利盧埃特與尼古拉谷故地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (23) Coyote and the Rolling Bowlder' (Thompson)

summary.en: In the Upper Uta'mqt country a bowlder at the foot of a cliff kills people by rolling on them, and Coyote learns which one it is by questioning his excrements. Standing below it, he hears it coming, drives his double-headed arrow-flaker into the ground with one end pointing uphill, and the bowlder shatters on the point — the patch of sharp white rock fragments that lies there now. Henceforth bowlders shall not kill people by rolling downhill: people shall be able to get out of their way.
summary.zh: 上利盧埃特之地，崖下巨石滾落殺人；郊狼問糞而知其為何石。立於石下，聞其滾近，將雙頭整箭器直插土中、一端朝上；巨石撞於鋒端，碎為粉末——今該處白色碎石一片即其遺。郊狼令：『自此滾石不得殺人，人皆得避之。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. A special form of the rolling-rock motif (cf. record coyote-rolling-rock). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling somewhere in the Upper Uta'mqt country, and came to a side-hill where there were bowlders at the foot of a cliff. Below, the side-hill was smooth. A bowlder lived here that killed people by rolling on them. Coyote did not know which one it was, and questioned his excrements; they told him, and it was a long distance above him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 10 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he was below it, he heard a noise and saw it coming. He stuck his double-headed arrow-flaker into the ground with one end pointing uphill, and when the bowlder hit the point, it broke into fragments — the patch of sharp fragments of white rock that is there now. He said: 'Henceforth bowlders shall not kill people by rolling downhill. People shall be able to get out of their way.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 10 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Coyote People

region.en: Interior Salish country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 內陸薩利什故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (26) The Coyote People' (Thompson)

summary.en: Coyote married a woman and had many children by her, and from these children descend the Salish tribes — the Thompson from one, the Shuswap from another, the Okanagon and Lillooet from others — which is why their languages are related. The Chilcotin, Carriers, Lower Fraser and Coast peoples are of different parentage, and for this reason the Thompson and Shuswap are often called 'Coyote people' in stories.
summary.zh: 郊狼娶妻生子甚多，內陸薩利什諸族皆其後裔：湯普森出自其一，舒什瓦普出自其二，奧卡諾根與利盧埃特又出自其他——故其語言同源。奇爾科廷、卡里埃、下弗雷澤與海岸諸族則另有始祖。因此故事中常稱湯普森人與舒什瓦普人為『郊狼子孫』。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Ethnogony; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote married a woman, and had many children by her. From these children are descended the Salish tribes: the Thompson are the descendants of one; the Shuswap, of another; Okanagon and Lillooet, of others. Therefore the languages of these tribes are related. The Chilcotin and Carriers must be of different parentage — some say they are the descendants of Deer or Bird people — and the Lower Fraser and Coast people are also different. On account of this story the Thompson and Shuswap are often called 'Coyote people' in stories.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 12 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Old-Coyote and the Separation of Languages

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (27) Old-Coyote and the Coyote People' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Old-Coyote, ancestor of all the Indians, had many wives, and from them descend the Thompson, Okanagon, Shuswap — and, as he travelled the world, the Salish, Kalispel, Nez Perce, Yakima, Blackfeet and all the interior tribes. Once all his descendants spoke one language like Shuswap; then Old-One separated the good from the bad, transformed the bad into coyotes, led the good forth, and settled them wide apart — so that when they met again they spoke different languages. Coyotes abound in the region of Old-Coyote's descendants and his travels, but nowhere else.
summary.zh: 老郊狼為印第安人之祖，多妻而子孫遍佈——湯普森、奧卡諾根、舒什瓦普，乃至薩利什、卡利斯佩爾、內茲珀斯、亞基馬、黑腳與內陸諸族皆其苗裔。其子孫初本同語（近舒什瓦普語）；後老者（Old-One）分善惡，化惡者為郊狼，率善者散居遠地，故重逢時言語已異。郊狼之多，唯見於老郊狼子孫之地與其遊蹤之處。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Language-separation ethnogony; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Old-Coyote (called 'Uncle Coyote' by some) was the ancestor of all the Indians. He had many wives; from some are descended the Thompson, from others the Okanagon, from still others the Shuswap. One of his sons had two wives, Lu'la and Tce'xa, varieties of ducks, and the latter had a simple-minded sister, the Frog, who followed her as her servant. Many of his sons had magical powers, and as Coyote travelled over a large part of the world he left children in many places: the Salish, Kalispel, Nez Perces, Yakima, and Blackfeet, and all the interior tribes, have sprung from Coyote's children. Because these tribes sprang from Coyote, they are called 'Coyote people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 12-13 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The descendants of Coyote spread over the country and occupied many parts that were not formerly inhabited. At one time they all spoke the same language, like Shuswap; some of them were bad people, but most were good. At a later date Old-One separated the good people from the bad: he transformed all the bad ones into coyotes, led the good ones forth, and made them settle at different places, widely apart. Afterwards, when the people met, they spoke different languages. For this reason coyotes abound in the region inhabited by Old-Coyote's descendants and in the country over which he travelled, but nowhere else.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 13 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Flood: The Stone Canoe on Zoke'ski
title.zh: 郊狼與洪水：佐克斯基山上的石舟

region.en: Thompson River, Zoke'ski mountain, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湯普森河佐克斯基山，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (28) Coyote and the Flood' (Thompson)

summary.en: A flood covers the whole country but the tops of the highest mountains — some say sent to put out a great world-fire, others to clean the earth. People and animals drown; some flee to peaks, some drift on logs, for no one knows how to make canoes. Only Coyote makes a canoe of horse-tails or grass, and with his friends drifts many days until they strike Zoke'ski mountain on the south side of the Thompson River, where the flood recedes. Leaving the canoe, he transforms it into stone — the thirty-foot stone canoe with three figures in it that stands near the mountain top — and the water-marks on the mountains, the mountain lakes and fish, and the tribes settled at Lytton and Nicola all descend from that voyage.
summary.zh: 洪水滔天，唯最高山尖未沒——或云為滅世界大火，或云為洗滌大地。人獸多溺斃；逃山頂者、抱木漂流者皆有，唯無人會造舟。獨郊狼以馬尾或草製舟，攜友漂流多日，撞上湯普森河南岸之佐克斯基山，水退。棄舟時化之為石——山頂附近今存三十尺石舟，內有三個人形，有的已消失。山中水痕、高湖之魚、利頓與尼古拉之移民，皆源於此舟。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Flood cluster parallel. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was living somewhere in the interior. He was a chief and father of the people; no one knows whence he came. For some reason a flood came, and covered the whole country except the tops of the highest mountains. Some say the flood came to put out a great fire which raged in the world; others say it was made to clean the earth. Many people and animals were drowned. Some fled to the high mountains, but the flood rose so rapidly that they were overtaken; some reached the tops and were saved. Some drifted about on logs, for no one knew how to make canoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 13 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Only Coyote made a canoe of horse-tails or grass, and he and some of his friends embarked in it. They drifted for many days, and at last struck a mountain on the south side of the Thompson River called Zoke'ski, where the flood receded rapidly. Coyote descended to the Thompson River and for a time took up his abode there; on leaving his canoe he transformed it into stone. It may still be seen near the top of the mountain: about thirty feet long, with figures of three persons in it, some of which have now disappeared. The water-marks of this flood may be seen on parts of the mountains; owing to the flood, water and fish are now found all over the mountains, which before were dry, with no lakes above the level of the low valleys. The survivors of the flood are the ancestors of the various tribes; some of the people from Coyote's canoe settled here and there — at Lytton, at Nicola, and other places.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 13 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Sesulia'n and Seku'lia: The Two Transformers
title.zh: 雙變形者：塞蘇利安與塞庫利亞

region.en: Fraser River from Shuswap country to the Thompson, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 弗雷澤河，自舒什瓦普至湯普森故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sesulia'n and Seku'lia' (Thompson, from Spences Bridge)

summary.en: Two good Transformers come down the Fraser from the Shuswap country, teaching the people arts and turning the proud to stone while helping the grateful. At Styne Creek a man mocks them and is petrified with his lodge and household; their footprints remain in the rock near Styne. They carry patterns of every tool drawn on hide, and teach fire-drills, cooking, stone-working, arrow-flaking, knives and harpoons; at Spuzzum they watch a man lower his son by a bark rope to snatch salmon bare-handed, and reveal to him, pattern by pattern, bark twine, the bag-net, the hoop and the dip-net — how to catch, cook and cure salmon. They disappear travelling east, and will return with Coyote when the world changes, when everything evil will be destroyed.
summary.zh: 兩位善之變形者自舒什瓦普順弗雷澤河而下，教民百藝：傲慢者化石，受教者受助。於斯泰因溪，一男子嘲之，遂與屋中人眾俱化石；溪畔林中今猶存二人足印。彼等攜繪於獸皮之百器圖樣，教鑽木取火、烹飪、治石、鑿鏃、刀叉魚叉諸術。至斯普澤姆，見一父以樹皮繩縋子徒手捉鮭而不得，遂一一示以圖樣：樹皮繩、網袋、網圈、抄網——教其捕鮭、烹鮭、藏鮭。二人東行而隱，將與郊狼同返；屆時世有大變，凡惡皆滅。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Transformer/culture-hero cycle with eschatological return; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Two Transformers, Sesulia'n and Seku'lia, came down the Fraser River from the Shuswap country. They were good men, and taught the people many arts: they transformed those who were proud, while they helped those who were grateful for advice and instruction. They reached Styne Creek at dusk. A number of people were living in an underground lodge just north of the creek, and their dogs began to howl when the Transformers approached. A man went out to see who was coming, and when he saw the Transformers he made fun of them; therefore they transformed him, the house, and the people into stone. When leaving this place, Sesulia'n left the mark of his right foot on a stone, and a little farther down the river Seku'lia left the mark of his left foot; both impressions of human feet may still be seen in the woods near Styne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 13-14 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Transformers taught people how to make tools and implements: they carried patterns drawn on hide of every object that people use, and taught how to make fire-drills, how to cook, how to work stone, flake arrow-heads and spears, how to make knives and harpoons. When they reached the Fraser Canyon near Spuzzum, they saw the river full of salmon, and across it a man lowering a boy by a cedar-bark rope to try to catch salmon with his hands — in vain. When the man wished that somebody would teach them how to catch the fish, the Transformers held up their hands above their heads, palms turned toward him, and he saw and understood them at once: first a pattern of bark twine, then a bag-net, then the hoop for a dip-net, and finally how to catch, cook, and cure salmon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 14 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Transformers went on to the boundary of the Lower Fraser tribe, and returned up the river to the Thompson tribe. Later on they left the country and disappeared; it is said they travelled through other countries to the east, teaching the people their arts. It is believed they will accompany Coyote when he returns: then there will be great changes on the earth, and many people will die — everything that is evil will be destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 14-15 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
